candidate.answerReason: Unfolding produces rectangles measuring 4 by 1, 4 by 2, and 4 by 1 inches. Their small-to-large perimeter ratio is 10/12 = 5/6.

methods.label: Track the cut when unfolding
methods.explanation:
First track the widths of the pieces. Folding the \(4\)-inch square in half makes a rectangle \(2\) inches wide and \(4\) inches tall. Cutting this folded rectangle in half parallel to the fold places the cut \(1\) inch from the fold.

Because the cut passes through both layers, unfolding produces two cut lines, one on each side of the original crease and \(1\) inch from it. The middle piece stays connected across the crease and has width \(1+1=2\) inches. Each outer piece has width \(1\) inch. All three pieces are still \(4\) inches tall.

A rectangle's perimeter is twice the sum of its length and width. Thus a small rectangle has perimeter \(2(4+1)=10\) inches, while the large rectangle has perimeter \(2(4+2)=12\) inches. The requested ratio is
\[
\frac{10}{12}=\boxed{\frac56},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
methods.levelReason: The solution uses elementary folding symmetry, equal halves, rectangle perimeters, and fraction reduction. No formal congruence or algebraic folding machinery is needed.

candidate.annotationRationale: The mathematical targets are calculating the resulting rectangle perimeters and comparing them as a ratio. The method uses elementary line symmetry to locate the two unfolded cuts. Rectangle side properties support the perimeter formula, equal halves determine the widths, and fraction reduction simplifies the final ratio. Ordered layer stacks and quadratic folding methods are not used.
